item.text: {"text":"HSTU already supports temporal adaptation within its backbone: learned relative-position and bucketed time-gap biases enter its pointwise SiLU attention. Meta’s implementation adds position and time-bucket parameters, providing a direct mechanism for learning which historical events remain relevant without imposing uniform decay. [HSTU paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152), [official implementation](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/generative_recommenders/research/modeling/sequential/hstu.py). Related 2025 work proposes lightweight session tokens, session-segment embeddings and temporal self-attention. These offer mechanisms to adapt inside one jointly trained HSTU; their reported improvements do not establish gains on this benchmark. [Session-aware recommendation](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/10902109).\n\nRecent work strengthens the motivation for distinguishing recent intent from persistent preference. HPGR (WWW 2026) identifies noise and missing session hierarchy in flat HSTU-style histories, introducing session-based representation learning and preference-guided sparse attention. Its industrial results support the hypothesis, but do not validate a particular Amazon session threshold. [HPGR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980). Practical experiment, inferred from these mechanisms: add a learned same-session/cross-session bias alongside bucketed elapsed-time bias, retaining causal HSTU attention and one checkpoint per category. Use timestamps only if aligned observed-history timestamps are accessible during both training and prediction; never require the unknown next-event timestamp. If prediction exposes item IDs alone, use learned positional recency or a jointly trained recent-history gate, explicitly treating these as order-based proxies. Long gaps may indicate intent drift; they do not establish that a purchase fulfilled a need."}
